This 55-year-old man presented with a painful, swollen ﬁnger and a fever (37.7°C).
What is likely to be found on microscopy of aspirated synovial ﬂuid?
options: Bipyramidal crystals that exhibit strong positive birefringence under polarised light
Rhomboid crystals that exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised light
Small, non-birefringent crystals visible only under electron microscopy
Needle-shaped crystals that exhibit strong negative birefringence under polarised light
explanation:
An acute attack of monoarticular arthritis is typical of gout. Agonising pain is usually accompanied by joint swelling, redness andtenderness, often with a low-grade fever. Urate crystals are needle-shaped, and exhibit strong negative birefringence underpolarised light microscopy.
The crystals described in the other answer options include:Calcium oxalate crystals - Bipyramidal crystals that exhibit strong positive birefringence under polarised lightCalcium pyrophosphate crystals - Rhomboid crystals that exhibit weak positive birefringence under polarised lightCalcium hydroxyapatite crystals - Small, non-birefringent crystals visible only under electron microscopy.

A 50-year-old Asian lady with severe rheumatoid arthritis has failed on most traditional DMARD treatments.
She is currently on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and for the last six months has been receiving regular infusions of the anti-TNF-alphamonoclonal antibody, inﬂiximab. Her joint disease has dramatically improved.
She now presents with fevers, pleuritic chest pain and a large left sided pleural effusion, but little evidence of joint synovitis.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely answer is TB.
All of the other answers are possible and need to be excluded.
A rheumatoid effusion is unlikely when peripheral joint disease is so well controlled.
Treatment with anti-TNF-alpha increases the risk of opportunistic infections and in particular, there is a signiﬁcant increase in therisk of TB reactivation in conjunction with inﬂiximab. Therefore patients are often screened for Hepatitis B, C, TB and HIV prior tocommencing inﬂiximab.

These lesions have appeared on her tongue four times in the past six months.
Which of the following HLA associations is found with increased frequency in patients with this disease?
explanation:
The slide shows ulcers on the tongue in a patient with a history of recurrent similar episodes, and a history of venous thrombosis.
The diagnosis is Behcet's disease which is a rare multisystem vasculitis.
Clinical features include the classical triad of:1. Recurrent oral ulceration2. Recurrent genital ulceration, and3. Iritis.
Arterial and venous thromboses are well recognised.
Patients may exhibit pathergy (development of pustules at venepuncture sites).

Examination reveals puffy swelling of the hands and wrists, associated with tenderness of the metacarpophalangeal joints. The chest x rayordered by the GP shows small bilateral pleural effusions.
Which of the following tests is characteristic of this patient's condition?
explanation:
Drug-induced (in this case procainamide) lupus erythematosus is typically mild, with arthritis, a photosensitive rash, serositis andmyalgia.
Kidneys and the central nervous system are usually spared, in contrast to systemic lupus erythematosus.
Most patients with procainamide-induced lupus produce antibodies to histone proteins.

An 82-year-old man presents with an isolated intracapsular fracture of his right neck of femur. He is alert and orientated, and states that hefelt dizzy and lost consciousness brieﬂy when he stood up. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and he takes furosemide for ankleoedema.
He has a soft mid-systolic murmur that is heard loudest over the second left intercostal space radiating to the carotid area. The second heartsound is muﬄed. He cannot leave his house unaided due to angina. He requires informal carer support to complete his activities of dailyliving due to breathlessness. His ECG shows the typical electrical criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, but no acute changes.
He has been booked onto the planned orthopaedic trauma list this afternoon.
What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Cancel surgery, and perform aortic valve replacement prior to hip ﬁxation
Perform surgery as planned, under general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring
Cancel surgery, manage the fracture conservatively with analgesics and traction
Cancel surgery, and arrange a transthoracic echocardiogram within ﬁve days
Perform surgery as planned, under a spinal anaesthetic
explanation:
This patient has clinical evidence of critical aortic stenosis (AS) with evidence of heart failure and left ventricular hypertrophy. He haspresented with a mechanism suggesting cardiogenic syncope. He is therefore likely to have a relatively ﬁxed cardiac output stateand will be at extremely high risk of morbidity and mortality in the perioperative period. A spinal anaesthetic will be a risky proceduredue to profound, uncontrolled and irreversible autonomic blockade. A cardiostable general anaesthetic with appropriate invasivemonitoring is more titratable and will be a safer option in these circumstances.
The patient's outcome is likely to be signiﬁcantly worse if surgery is delayed. Although delay may be acceptable to amendimmediately

As her disease is still active, she is commenced on oral cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day for six months), and subsequently on azathioprine.
Of which of the following is she most at risk?MARKED
explanation:
Cyclophosphamide causes premature ovarian failure and infertility in both men and women.
The risk increases with increasing doses of cyclophosphamide and is greater in younger patients.
Cyclophosphamide treatment does not lead to breast cancer, hyperthyroidism, ovarian cancer, or venous thromboembolism.

This patient is attempting to dorsiﬂex his right wrist.
There is a small area of sensory loss on the dorsum of the right hand, overlying the metacarpophalangeal joints of the right thumb and rightﬁrst ﬁnger.
What is the likely cause of this injury?
options: Fracture involving the midshaft of the humerus
Fracture involving the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
Fracture involving the medial epicondyle of the humerus
explanation:
This clinical description and photograph is suggestive of radial nerve palsy giving rise to wrist drop.
The typical causes of wrist drop are damage to the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus in a midshaft fracture, and also asa result of acute compression. This is commonly caused by the "Saturday night palsy", when the affected subject falls asleep withtheir arm over the side of a chair.
Ulnar nerve injury is caused by compression at the medial epicondyle.

A 33-year-old teacher presented with a three week history of pain, swelling, and stiffness in his ankles. He had a cough and mild exertionalshortness of breath.
On examination, his ankles were warm, tender, and swollen. Chest examination was normal. FBC, U&E, and LFTs were normal. Anti-CCPantibodies and rheumatoid factor were negative. CRP was high at 38 mg/L, and a serum ACE was 133 (normal 0-65) units.
Chest radiograph showed bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and reticulo-nodular shadows in lung ﬁelds.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sarcoidosis is suggested by the presence of:ankle arthritisbilateral hilar adenopathypulmonary ﬁbrosis, anda high serum ACE level.
Inﬂammatory arthritis in sarcoidosis typically targets the ankle joint.
Rheumatoid arthritis is unlikely as he is sero-negative for both rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP antibodies, and there is noinvolvement of the small joints of hands, and feet.
Atypical pneumonia, lymphoma, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection do not lead to this constellation of symptoms, signs, andlaboratory results.

A 36-year-old Turkish man presents with superﬁcial thrombophlebitis in his leg veins.
On enquiry, there is a history of recurrent episodes of oral and genital ulcers in the last year. Some of these ulcers have left scars. He has ahistory of anterior uveitis.
Recent blood tests show a normocytic normochromic anaemia, normal LFTs, UE&C, and a raised ESR (66 mm/hr). A venous Doppler revealedbelow knee deep venous thrombosis.
On which of the following medicines should he be commenced?
explanation:
This patient has Behçet's disease.
Behçet's syndrome is a systemic vasculitis with an unknown aetiology, which affects small and large vessels (venous and arterial).More than 60% of patients are HLA-B51, and there is an increased prevalence in the Mediterranean countries.
It is commonly associated with mucocutaneous manifestations (oro-genital ulceration, erythema nodosum), ocular disease,gastrointestinal involvement and neurological features. Venous thrombosis is a common complication. Thrombosis of major vesselslike the vena cava and suprahepatic veins may occur but is rare. Similarly, inﬂammation of arterial wall may occur, leading to theformation of aneurysm and/or occlusion. Thrombo-embolism is rare as the thrombi are adherent to the vessel wall.
Current EULAR guidelines recommend that corticosteroids in conjunction with immunosuppressants like azathioprine,cyclosporine, and cyclophosphamide may be used in those with venous or arterial involvement. These recommendations are basedon the widely held belief that the cause of clot is inﬂammation of the vessel wall.
DVT in Behçet's adhere to the vessel wall and do not result in emboli. Pulmonary embolism is therefore rare despite a high frequencyof venous thrombosis.
Evidence is lacking for the use of anticoagulation, antiﬁbrinolytics, and antiplatelet agents, and routine use of these is notrecommended. Another reason to avoid these agents is the possibility of a coexisting pulmonary arterial aneurysm, which mightresult in fatal bleeding.

A 20-year-old woman presents with typical erythema nodosum. She has a low grade fever and bilateral ankle arthritis but no other symptomsand has no medical history. There is no history of travel abroad and she is on no medication.
Which of the following would be the most appropriate investigation for this patient to aid diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum is commonly idiopathic.
It can also be related to streptococcal infections, acute sarcoidosis or related to drugs such as the oral contraceptive pill,sulphonamides and penicillins.
Rarer causes include inﬂammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis, Behçet's disease and other connective tissue disorders.
In this case, a chest x ray would be the most helpful investigation as this may identify bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy which togetherwith a bilateral ankle arthropathy would strongly support a diagnosis of acute sarcoidosis.
Investigation of the bowel is unlikely to help in the absence of any bowel symptoms.
Viral titres and ESR are non-speciﬁc.

An 80-year-old lady was reviewed in the outpatient clinic.
She was diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica eighteen months previously when she presented with bilateral shoulder stiffness andgeneralised myalgia; the ESR on presentation had been 60 mm/1st hour (0-30).
She was started on prednisolone 15 mg daily along with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and she responded well, with resolution ofher symptoms within one week. However, her symptoms have persistently relapsed when the dose of prednisolone has been reduced belowher current dose of 12.5 mg of prednisolone daily.
How should her disease be managed?
options: Continue the current dose of prednisolone
Continue to taper the prednisolone and treat any symptoms with non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs
Increase the dose of prednisolone and add a bisphosphonate
Continue the current dose of prednisolone and start methotrexate
explanation:
Corticosteroids remain the mainstay of treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).
The starting dose depends on patient's weight and severity of symptoms. The optimum duration of treatment is uncertain and islargely guided by response to therapy.
Calcium and vitamin D supplementation should be initiated for all patients with PMR who are starting corticosteroid therapy.Bisphosphonates should be added for long term steroid therapy.
The usual starting dose is 15 mg prednisolone per day. Patients should expect relief of symptoms within 24-72 hours. The doseshould be increased if symptoms are not well controlled within one week. The effective starting dose should be maintained for twoto four weeks after the patient becomes asymptomatic.
Generally, the daily dose can be lowered by 1.0-2.5 mg every two to four weeks to ﬁnd the minimum dose needed to maintainsymptom suppression. Once the patient is reduced to 10 mg per day, the daily dose can be tapered by 1 mg every four weeks.
Tapering should be guided by clinical response.
Normalisation of inﬂammatory markers (especially erythrocyte sedimentation rate [ESR]) are helpful but should not set theguidelines for decreasing or stopping the treatment. An isolated increase of ESR without symptoms during the course of treatmentis not a valid reason to increase corticosteroid dose; however, a temporary delay in dosage reduction may be necessary.

A 25-year-old woman with SLE (antinuclear antibody positive [1:6400], anti-dsDNA antibody positive) presents with a few months history offeeling generally unwell, tiredness, malar rash, and marked pedal oedema. There is no history of breathlessness.
On examination, the BP is 130/90 mm Hg, and there are 4+ protein and 2+ haematuria in her urine. She has normal heart sounds and,reduced breath sounds at both lung bases. 
Bloods show a creatinine of 147 and she undergoes a renal biopsy which shows widespread deposition of IgG within the glomeruli.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of these ﬁndings?
explanation:
The combination of peripheral oedema and marked proteinuria in this patient indicates the presence of nephrotic syndrome
The renal manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are highly variable, ranging from mild asymptomatic proteinuriaand/or haematuria to rapidly progressive uraemia. The various presentations are diﬃcult to classify into clinical syndromes andhistological classes. Although lupus nephritis affects a third of patients early in the disease it is frequently unrecognised untilnephritic and/or nephrotic syndrome with renal failure occur.
Histologically, a number of different types of renal disease are recognised in SLE, with immune-complex mediated glomerulardisease being the most common. The up to date International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society 2003 classiﬁcationdivides these into six different patterns:I - minimal mesangialII - mesangial proliferativeIII - focalIV - diffuseV - membranousVI - advanced sclerosis
Glomeruli appear normal by light microscopy in minimal mesangial lupus nephritis, but immunoﬂuorescence demonstratesmesangial immune deposits.

A 65-year-old woman with SLE is diagnosed with class IV SLE nephritis.
The renal physician plans to start her on i.v. methylprednisolone (1 gm/day for three days) followed by oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, andfortnightly i.v. cyclophosphamide.
Which of the following drugs does not need to be co-prescribed with these two agents?
explanation:
This patient is at risk of P. jirovecii pneumonia. She requires co-trimoxazole for prophylaxis against P. jirovecii pneumonia.
She is on steroids and cyclophosphamide both of which increase the risk of P. jirovecii pneumonia.
Among other things, corticosteroids cause peptic ulcer, and osteoporosis.
Therefore she requires omeprazole for gastro-protection from corticosteroids, and she requires both a bisphosphonate, and calcium+ vitamin D for prophylaxis against osteoporosis as she is ≥ 65-years-old.

A 25-year-old Caucasian farmer presents to the outpatient department complaining of a two month history of lower back pain which is worstﬁrst thing in the morning. He reports intermittent pain and swelling of his right ankle, although he did sustain an injury to this whilst runninga year ago.
Two weeks ago he was seen in the Emergency department with a painful red eye for which he was treated with eye drops. He is a heavysmoker of 45 cigarettes a day and consumes ﬁve pints of beer every weekend. He denies any skin rashes or mucosal ulceration. His mothersuffered from rheumatoid arthritis and his father had severe gout. On direct questioning he admits to being diagnosed with chlamydia fourmonths ago.
On examination his right ankle was swollen at the site of Achilles' tendon insertion but all the other joints were unremarkable. Flexion of thelumbar spine was reduced.
What is the most likely diagnoses in this man?
explanation:
The history is most suggestive of a spondyloarthritis.
This is a group of related but phenotypically distinct disorders including:Ankylosing spondylitisReactive arthritisPsoriatic arthritis, andA subgroup of juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
HLA-B27 is a predisposing factor for all these disorders and is present in 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis and 75% withreactive arthritis. It is present in only 8% of the normal Caucasian population.
Ankylosing spondylitis is a very disabling form of spondyloarthritis and its diagnosis should always be considered in these cases. Themain symptom is inﬂammatory spinal and with time ankylosing and spinal immobilitiy develops. The pathology mainly affects theentheses. TNF-antagonists are the major treatment advance although physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agentsstill have a role.

A 23-year-old teacher with ankylosing spondylitis presents with headache. She has a painful right eye, and also reports cloudy vision.
On examination, the eye is red, photophobic, pupils are small, and the pupillary reﬂex is sluggish. Although the visual ﬁelds are normal, shereports cloudy vision. Recent FBC, UEC and liver function tests are normal.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Patients with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are at risk of uveitis.
Blepharitis (inﬂammation of eyelid) and conjunctivitis lead to mild symptoms.
Corneal melts (perforating corneal ulceration) is the end stage of keratitis which is seen typically in rheumatoid arthritis. Patientswith corneal melts have corneal opacities and ulceration which leads to scotomata.
Scleritis presents as dusky blue discoloration of the sclera, with associated pain, and tenderness, but does not lead to photophobia,or sluggish pupillary reﬂex.

stem:
A 33-year-old teacher presents with a three week history of dry cough, low grade fever, and erythematous nodular lesions on the cheek,nose, forehead and chin.
Systemic examination is normal.
A chest x ray showed bilateral hilar adenopathy. The lesions on her face were biopsied and showed multiple non-caseating granulomata.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has got lupus pernio, a skin manifestation that is speciﬁc to sarcoidosis.
Differential diagnosis of bilateral hilar adenopathy includes:SarcoidosisLymphomaTuberculosisPneumoconiosisBerylliosis, andFungal diseases like histoplasmosis.
Unlike in sarcoidosis, the granulomata in tuberculosis show caseating necrosis.
The differential diagnosis of lupus pernio includes:Granulomatosis with polyangiitisLymphoma cutis, andCutaneous lupus.
The clinical presentation helps differentiate some lesions, but a biopsy may be required.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis patients usually present with symptoms of sinusitis, otitis, or nasal ulceration. The skin lesionsinclude ulcers, nodules, and granuloma formation.

stem:
A 62-year-old woman with knee OA and a history of peptic ulcers, presents with a one week history of worsening left knee pain. The pain isincreased by walking, climbing stairs, and is debilitating her. There is no history of knee swelling, or injury.
The pain is partially controlled by co-codamol (30/500 mg) two tablets up to four times a day, NSAID gel, and fentanyl patches.
On examination, she is overweight. There is crepitus in her right knee and no knee effusion. 
What is the next step in her management?
explanation:
This patient is having a ﬂare of osteoarthritis (OA) related knee pain.
There is no role for acupuncture or oral corticosteroids in controlling such pain.
Such ﬂares are common, and may be controlled by opiates, non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs)/Coxibs or intra-articularcorticosteroid injections. Of these, intra-articular long acting corticosteroid injections are most effective.
The need for intra-articular long acting corticosteroid injections should be guided by symptoms, and not by the presence or absenceof joint effusion.

A 22-year-old man with known hereditary angioneurotic oedema (HAO) presents with a recurrent fever, arthralgia and a rash on the face andthe upper chest.
Despite treatment for his HAO, he has always been troubled by recurrent attacks and has required adrenaline on several occasions. His C4levels have been persistently reduced secondary to his HAO.
What is the most likely cause for his current symptoms?
explanation:
HAO is characterised by deﬁciency of C1 esterase inhibitor.
This leads to persistent activation of the classical complement pathway and C4 levels are frequently low secondary to activation andconsumption.
If treatment fails to normalise the C4 levels and they remain persistently low; these patients are at an increased risk of developingSLE.

An 82-year-old gentleman is referred to your outpatient clinic by his GP. He gives a two month history of proximal muscle stiffness, especiallyin the morning. He denies any weakness.
What is the next best investigation?
explanation:
The brief history is suggestive of polymyalgia rheumatica: proximal muscle stiffness but not weakness in an elderly patient.Weakness and muscle pain are the predominant features of polymyositis.
While each of the other tests listed might be relevant in the broad work-up of this patient, a high ESR would prompt immediatetreatment with steroids.
Polymyalgia is often associated with giant cell arteritis - prompt treatment may prevent blindness.

A 37-year-old woman who recently started gardening presents with pain on the lateral aspect of her right wrist. This is worsened by making aﬁst, and by using heavy gardening tools.
On examination, there is tenderness, and swelling around the lateral margin of the right wrist, extending a few centimeters proximally.Finkelstein's test is positive. Recent FBC, UEC, LFTs and rheumatoid factor have been negative. MARKEDMARKEDMARKED 
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
DeQuervain's tenosynovitis occurs in the ﬁrst extensor compartment on the back of the thumb. It involves abductor pollicis longusand extensor pollicis brevis tendons. There is localised pain, worsened by aggravating motion and swelling. Localised tendernessmay be present.
Finkelstein's test - exacerbation of symptoms on ﬂexion of thumb, and ulnar deviation of wrist - may be present but is notpathognomonic of DeQuervain's tenosynovitis.
Intersection syndrome is tenosynovitis of the extensor carpi radialis tendons, where these tendons are crossed by abductor pollicislongus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons. The pain and swelling is present 4 cm proximal to the wrist joint.
Preiser's disease and Kienbock's disease are avascular necrosis of scaphoid and lunate bones respectively, and present with pain andswelling in the wrist joint.
Dupuytren's contracture is a condition of nodular hypertrophy and contractures of the superﬁcial palmar fascia. Patients presentwith pitting, and nodule and thickening of the fascia of the hand. MARKEDMARKED

He drinks 6 units of alcohol/week and has just returned from USA. There is no signiﬁcant past or family history except that his sister haspsoriasis.

A 68-year-old woman presents with pain at the base of her right thumb. There is tenderness and swelling of the right ﬁrst carpometacarpaljoint.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The ﬁrst carpometacarpal joint is a frequent site of osteoarthritis in postmenopausal women. Clinical features include tenderness,stiffness, crepitus, swelling and pain on abduction of the thumb. Squaring of the hand, caused by swelling, radial subluxation of themetacarpal and atrophy of the thenar muscles, is a characteristic clinical sign.
Scaphoid fractures are relatively common, typically occurring following a fall onto outstretched hand. The proximal portion lacks itsown blood supply, so avascular necrosis can occur if a fracture leaves it isolated from the remainder of the scaphoid. This producespain and tenderness of the radial side of the wrist, classically in the anatomical snuffbox rather than the base of the thumb,exacerbated by wrist movement.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis disease is a common pathology which consists of a stenosing tenosynovitis of the ﬁrst dorsalcompartment of the wrist. It typically presents with pain on the radial aspect of the wrist, with associated swelling and tenderness.Treatment is with splinting, with or without corticosteroid injection.
Reference:1. Ilyas AM, at al. De quervain tenosynovitis of the wrist. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2007;15:757-64.2. Peter JB, Marmor L. Osteoarthritis of the ﬁrst carpometacarpal joint. Calif Med. 1968;109:116-20.

A 29-year-old woman was referred to clinic for an opinion regarding a three month history of fatigue, generalised weakness, easy bruisingand joint pains. On examination she appeared pale.
The spleen was palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. The remainder of the examination was normal.
Investigations showed:
Haemoglobin95 g/L(115-165)
MCV 95 fL (80-96)
White cell count2.1 ×10/L (4-11)
Platelets 55 ×10/L (150-400)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The combination of pancytopenia, arthralgia and splenomegaly makes SLE the most likely diagnosis.
Acute leukaemias are associated with elevated white cell counts often accompanied by leukaemia and thrombocytopenia;hepatosplenomegaly is usually a feature of ALL rather than AML.
ITP may be associated with thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly, but is not associated with penias of myeloid and lymphoid celllines.
Patients with longstanding rheumatoid arthritis may develop Felty's syndrome (leucopenia and splenomegaly; often accompaniedby anaemia and thrombocytopenia) but this follows years of active rheumatoid disease.

A 66-year-old man has had a painful, swollen right knee and diﬃculty walking over the last three days. He has had two self-limiting episodesof severe pain and swelling in the right big toe in the last year.
A knee aspirate shows leucocytes but no organisms on Gram stain, and negatively birefringent crystals on polarised light microscopy. Recentblood tests show normal renal function, and a raised serum urate 452 µmol/L (210-415 µmol/L).
What is the next step in his long term management, once the current episode of acute synovitis has settled?
explanation:
The British Society of Rheumatology guidelines state that the plasma urate should be maintained below 300 µmol/L in themanagement of gout.
Drug therapy (allopurinol in the ﬁrst instance) is indicated to achieve this if:A second attack occurs within one year of the initial presentationTophi are presentThe patient has renal insuﬃciencyThere are also uric acid stones, andDiuretics cannot be stopped.
However, it is important to remember that commencement of uric acid lowering drug therapy should be delayed until one to twoweeks after the initial episode has resolved. Colchicine should be co-prescribed for the ﬁrst six months.
Febuxostat is a non-purine selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase. that reduces serum uric acid concentration. NICE guidancerecommends its use only in patients who are intolerant of allopurinol or for whom allopurinol is contraindicated.
Oral, intramuscular or intra-articular corticosteroids are effective in the control of acute gout, however prolonged use is associatedwith signiﬁcant side effects and they are therefore not indicated in the long term management.

Investigations revealed:

A 62-year-old woman with knee OA, past history of peptic ulcers, and ischaemic heart disease presents with a one year history of worseningbilateral, anterior knee pain. The pain is increased by walking and climbing stairs.
There is no history of knee swelling. The pain is partially controlled by co-codamol (30/500 mg), two tablets up to four times a day, NSAID gel,and capsaicin cream.
On examination, she is overweight. There is crepitus and during active and passive movement of both knees. There is no knee effusion.
What is the next step in her management?
explanation:
This patient has knee pain resistant to several simple analgesics. The next step in her treatment is to start her on stronger opiates.
There is not enough evidence that acupuncture or chondroitin sulphate is clinically or cost effective in osteoarthritis (OA).
Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be used for short term pain relief of severe symptomatic knee OA, however, theuse of NSAIDs for long term pain control in OA is discouraged.
Long term oral NSAIDs are potentially dangerous as they may lead to renal failure, ﬂuid retention, peptic ulcers, and arecontraindicated in this patient as she has a history of peptic ulcers.
Cox-2 inhibitors have a much lower risk of gastrointestinal bleed. However, as they increase the risk of cardiovascular events, theyshould not be prescribed to those with cardiovascular disease, or in those with high risk of cardiovascular disease.

A 25-year-old Caucasian farmer presents to the outpatient department complaining of a two month history of generalised aches and pains.
He used to be an active runner but says a hip injury forced him to give up competitive running a year ago. Two years ago he was seen in theEmergency department with a painful red eye for which he was treated with eye drops. He is a heavy smoker of 45 cigarettes a day andconsumes ﬁve pints of beer every weekend. He denies any skin rashes or mucosal ulceration. His mother suffered from rheumatoid arthritisand his father had severe gout.
On examination, the left ﬁrst metatarsophalangeal joint was swollen and tense, but all the other joints were unremarkable. Rotation of thelumbar spine was restricted.
Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
options: Examination of joint ﬂuid for crystals
explanation:
A history of joint pains, in particular that of the lumbar spine, ocular involvement (uveitis) and the absence of mucosal ulceration in amale would suggest a differential diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis.
The earliest radiographic change in ankylosing spondylitis is usually sacroiliitis, which may also be seen in reactive arthritis.
HLA-B27 antigen typing is present in 90% of patients with ankylosing spondylitis and 75% with reactive arthritis.
However, it is present in only 8% of the normal Caucasian population.

A 54-year-old patient with tophaceous gout developed hypersensitivity reaction to allopurinol tablets. He is offered long-term urate-loweringtreatment with febuxostat.
Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of febuxostat?
explanation:
Febuxostat is a non-purine, selective inhibitor of xanthine oxidase; unlike allopurinol, which is a purine analogue inhibitor of xanthineoxidase.
Uricosuric agents, like probenecid and benzbromarone, work by blocking the anion exchanger URAT-1 at the apical brush bordermembrane of the proximal tubule in kidneys.
They also block urate reabsorption at the basolateral membrane of these cells by blocking GLUT 9 - the electrogenic glucose andfructose transport facilitator.

A 64-year-old patient with sero-positive erosive RA has active inﬂammatory arthritis despite treatment with methotrexate (20 mg/week), andsulfasalazine (1 gram bd).
He is offered treatment with biological agents. Of the various options available, he chooses to stat abatacept.
Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of abatacept?
explanation:
Abatacept is a cytotoxic lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA 4) homologue - licensed for RA treatment.
Adalimumab, etanercept, inﬂiximab, golimumab, and certolizumab are anti-TNF alpha agents.
Rituximab is an anti-CD 20 antibody - licensed for RA treatment.
Anakinra is an anti-IL 1 antibody.

A 65-year-old woman presents with deteriorating wheeze and dyspnoea.
She has been diagnosed with asthma over the last 15 years and is treated with inhaled salbutamol, inhaled ﬂuticasone and has receivednumerous courses of prednisolone. Currently, she is receiving 15 mg of prednisolone daily as a reducing dose.
Four years ago, she had also received cyclical hormone replacement therapy (HRT) for post-menopausal ﬂushes but this was stopped afterone year of therapy when she developed a deep vein thrombosis.
What treatment would you select as prophylaxis against osteoporosis?
explanation:
This patient is at high risk of developing osteoporosis being post-menopausal and receiving high doses of steroids.
Of the therapies listed the most appropriate is the bisphosphonate, alendronate. NICE guidelines suggest the use ofbisphosphonates where steroids are used over the longer term for the prevention of osteoporosis. This treatment should be for 3-5years and patients should be made aware that it is not preventative but reduces risk.
Calcitonin is administered subcutaneously and is not appropriate.
Raloxifene is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) and is an appropriate therapy for the prevention and treatment ofpost-menopausal osteoporosis but like HRT may be associated with an increased risk of thromboembolism and should not be usedin this case.
Calcium and vitamin D are useful adjuncts but would not prevent steroid induced osteoporosis.
Reference:
NICE. Osteoporosis: assessing the risk of fragility fracture (CG146).

A 47-year-old woman with longstanding diabetes presents with a painful, stiff left shoulder of three weeks duration.  The pain is dull, achingand present at rest. Shoulder movements are reduced. There is no history of trauma, temperature, or night pain.
On examination, the shoulder movements are globally restricted. There is no evidence of shoulder effusion. Cervical spine movements arenormal. Recent FBC, UEC, LFT, and bone proﬁle are normal.
What is the most likely cause of her shoulder symptoms?
explanation:
This patient has adhesive capsulitis. Adhesive capsulitis (synonym, frozen shoulder) is common in diabetics.
In this condition there is a fairly acute onset of dull pain, and global restriction of shoulder movements. Pain is frequently present atrest. External rotation is the most severely affected movement.
Subacromial bursitis presents with shoulder pain when trying to reach above the head. During examination, pain is present in themid arc of shoulder abduction. There is usually no rest pain. Active shoulder abduction is limited by pain. However, there is full rangeof shoulder abduction passively.
Rotator cuff tears present with symptoms similar to subacromial impingement. There may be weakness in speciﬁc shouldermovements in full thickness rotator cuff tears. 
Osteoarthritis at glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints usually presents with gradually worsening, generalised shoulder, orshoulder tip pain, in older people, or in those with physically demanding jobs.

He is on aspirin, amlodipine, metformin, and citalopram.
During routine tests, his serum urate was checked. This was 521 μ mol/L (210-415).
What is the next step in his management?
explanation:
Uric acid is the ﬁnal product of purine metabolism. Raised levels are most commonly associated with gout, but more recently theyhave been identiﬁed as a marker for a number of metabolic and haemodynamic abnormalities (including ischaemic heart disease,diabetes mellitus, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia).
Blood levels depend of the rate of breakdown and excretion, and most cases of hyperuricaemia are associated with defectiveelimination.
Causes of hyperuricaemia include:
Underexcretion:Renal impairmentMetabolic syndromeDrugs, e.g. diuretics, low-dose aspirin, cyclosporin, tacrolimus, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, levodopa, nicotinic acidAcidosisPre-eclampsia and eclampsiaHypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidismSarcoidosisFamilial juvenile gouty nephropathyChronic lead intoxicationTrisomy 21Idiopathic.

A 40-year-old insulin-dependent man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with an acutely erythematous and swollen right mid footwhich he has experienced for the last three weeks. He drinks alcohol socially, and has had no recent injuries to the foot.
On examination, the mid foot is warm. Pedal pulses are intact. There is sensory loss in a glove and stocking distribution bilaterally.
Recent blood tests show a normal FBC, CRP, and UEC, and a foot radiograph is normal.
What is the next step in his management?
explanation:
In patients with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy, a red hot swollen foot should raise suspicion of Charcotneuroarthropathy.
Charcot neuropathy presents as a warm, swollen, erythematous foot and ankle, and infection is important to exclude. The majority ofpatients are in their 50-60s, and they often present in the latter stages of the disease. It can occur in association with a variety ofconditions, including leprosy, poliomyelitis, rheumatoid arthritis, although today the most common cause is diabetes mellitus.
The pathophysiology of Charcot neuroarthropathy is not completely understood, but is thought to start with peripheral neuropathy.The lack of pain sensation may mean that patients subject the foot joints (commonly the mid foot) to stress injuries that lead to theCharcot process. It is important to note however that about half of patients present with pain.
Four stages of Charcot neuropathy are recognised:Stage 0 (inﬂammation) - characterised by erythema and oedema, but no structural changes.Stage 1 (development) - bone resorption, fragmentation and joint dislocation. Swelling, warmth and erythema persist butthere are also radiographic changes such as debris formation at the articular margins, osseous fragmentation and jointdisruption.Stage 2 (coalescence) - bony consolidation, osteosclerosis and fusion are all seen on plain radiographs.Stage 3 (reconstruction) - osteogenesis, decreased osteosclerosis, progressive fusion. Healing and new bone formation occur,and the deformity becomes permanent.

A 70-year-old retired sea captain develops weakness of the shoulders and hips over a four month period. He has also noticed weak ﬁngerﬂexors with normal strength in straightening them. He has had some diﬃculty swallowing liquids.
There is no past medical history, apart from a sexually transmitted disease picked up in the South Paciﬁc some forty years before. This wastreated with antibiotics and he is not sure of the diagnosis.
He smokes a pipe and drinks one or two tots of rum at the weekend.
A creatine kinase level comes back at 120.
Which investigation is most likely to give a deﬁnite diagnosis?
explanation:
The diagnosis is inclusion body myositis (IBM). This is an inﬂammatory condition that affects the over 50s.
Proximal muscles and ﬁnger ﬂexors are predominantly involved, but distal muscle groups may also be involved. The onset of muscleweakness in IBM is generally gradual (over months or years).
IBM occurs more frequently in men than women. Creatine kinase (CK) may be normal.
Jo 1 titres are often raised in dermatomyositis associated with lung disease.
Electromyogram (EMG) shows a similar pattern in polymyositis and IBM - small short duration motor unit arrythmias can complicatepolymyositis and dermatomyositis, but not IBM.
There is no association of IBM with malignancy.
Polymyositis and dermatomyositis show a much better response to steroids than IBM.
Biopsy in IBM shows intranuclear or cytoplasmic tuboﬁlaments on electron microscopy.

She is on methotrexate 20 mg/week and folic acid 5 mg/day. Her arthritis is well controlled, with no swollen or tender joints.

explanation:
Patients with RA frequently have eye complications. These include:Episcleritis (red, tender, superﬁcial painful lesions, well localised)Scleritis (blue dusky, tender, painful lesions)Keratitis (photophobia, visual disturbance), andCorneal ulcers.
In severe cases there may also be scleromalacia perforans or corneal melts.
Felty's syndrome is a triad of splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis, and pancytopenia (predominantly neutropenia) in someone withlongstanding seropositive RA.

A 22-year-old patient with SLE for last six years presents with sudden onset shortness of breath for last two days.
On examination, the pulse is 105/min, BP 110/70 mm Hg, SaO of 93% on air.
Other organ system examination is normal. FBC, U&E, INR are normal. D-dimers are positive. A chest radiograph and ECG are normal.
Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) are at risk of anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome (APAS).
APAS is present if the patient hasAnticardiolipin antibodies or lupus anticoagulant on two occasions over a period of 12 weeks
and either has hadA thrombus, or A history of recurrent less than 10 week pregnancy loss orOne pregnancy loss greater than 10 weeks in gestation
when other causes of pregnancy loss have been excluded. 
Patients with APAS and another autoimmune condition are said to have secondary APAS, while those with APAS where noassociated autoimmune condition can be identiﬁed are said to have primary APAS.
Other causes of shortness of breath in SLE, like shrinking lung syndrome, and pneumonitis do not present acutely, and thereforepulmonary function test or HRCT are unlikely to be of any beneﬁt.

A 65-year-old man presented with a four week history of pleuritic chest pain associated with shortness of breath and dry cough. He alsoreported weight loss of nearly 10 kg in the past six months.
He had a past history of myocardial infarction 20 years earlier from which he had made a good recovery. He did not suffer from any exertionalchest pain subsequently.
He lived alone and had not seen his general practitioner for two years. He seldom saw his general practitioner, but had attended the surgerytwice recently with mild recurrent pain in his left knee that responded well to treatment with simple analgesia. He was an ex-smoker of 15cigarettes per day, having given up smoking 10 years previously. His only medication was aspirin.
On examination of his chest he had reduced expansion, dull percussion note and decreased breath sounds on the right. A chest x rayconﬁrmed a right-sided pleural effusion.
Analysis of a pleural aspirate revealed:
Pleural ﬂuid protein content42 g/L
Pleural ﬂuid glucose2.0 mmol/L
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The pleural ﬂuid protein is greater than 35 g/L which demonstrates it is an exudate and effectively excludes cardiac failure.
If pleural ﬂuid protein is 25-35 g/L then Light's criteria are more accurate in determining whether the effusion is an exudate ortransudate. It is an exudate if one or more of the following criteria are met1. Pleural ﬂuid protein divided by serum protein greater than  0.52. She is otherwise well, is a non-smoker drinks about ﬁve units of alcohol weekly and has a healthy diet.
Examination reveals a ﬁt thin female with a BMI of 18 kg/m, her blood pressure is 122/88 mmHg and breast examination is normal.
Which of the following would you recommend for her?
explanation:
This patient has a risk for osteoporosis being thin and recently having had oophrectomy.
Department of Health guidelines would support the use of oestrogen replacement as ﬁrst-line therapy in such patients.
Unopposed oestrogen therapy is most appropriate as the patient has had a hysterectomy and combined hormone replacementtherapy (HRT) is unnecessary.
Tibolone, raloxiﬁne and bisphosphonates are recommended as second-line agents where HRT may be poorly tolerated or contra-indicated.
Although things are continuing to change with regard to publications such as Women's Health Study and Million Women Study, thefact remains that in symptomatic patients, HRT offers the best therapeutic option and in the absence of any cardiovascular riskfactors is recommended. The guidelines state that hormone therapy be used at the lowest doses for the shortest duration needed toachieve treatment goals.

On examination, his temperature is 38.8 ℃ , BP is 90/60 mm Hg, and pulse is 110/min. The right ankle is warm, tender, and there is a tensejoint effusion. You have collected bloods including blood cultures, and have started ﬂuid resuscitation.MARKED
Which of the following is the most appropriate step in his management?
options: Administer i.v. ﬂucloxacillin, and arrange bone scan
Administer i.v. ﬂucloxacillin, and arrange joint aspiration urgently
Administer i.v. ﬂucloxacillin, and arrange MRI of right ankle
Administer i.v. ﬂucloxacillin, and arrange joint aspiration next day
explanation:
Septic arthritis must be excluded in an individual with acute monoarthritis.
Septic arthritis may be oligo- or polyarticular in the immunosuppressed, and may present without pyrexia.
Joint aspiration, followed by microscopy and culture of the synovial ﬂuid is critical to the diagnosis of septic arthritis, and should becollected prior to giving antibiotics. However, this patient has septic shock, and administration of antibiotics takes precedence overcollection of synovial ﬂuid, especially if the latter is likely to delay the administration of antibiotics.
MRI will show a wide range of non-speciﬁc changes in this scenario, for example, effusion, synovial proliferation, bone marrowoedema, none of which is speciﬁc to septic arthritis.
A bone scan will show increased uptake at the inﬂamed joint, and will not allow differentiation between infective and other causes.

A 67-year-old Caucasian with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with monthly i.v. cyclophosphamide and oral prednisolone for sixmonths.
His vasculitis is well controlled, and the plan is to commence him on azathioprine.
He has normal full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, and liver function tests.
What screening test is required before commencing him on azathioprine?
explanation:
Blood for thiopurine methyltransferase should be checked prior to starting azathioprine.
Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) in vivo. 6-MP may be metabolised to inactive 6-methyl mercaptopurine, ormay be methylated to active compounds by the enzyme thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT).
Among Caucasians, 89% percent have normal or high levels, 11% have low levels, and 0.3% people are deﬁcient in TPMT. 
As a result, if azathioprine is given to those deﬁcient in TPMT (undetectable levels), it results in severe side effects, for example,myelosuppression.
Patients with normal or high levels of TPMT may be safely commenced on azathioprine, while those with low levels of TPMT may begiven low doses of azathioprine under expert supervision.
